claim: Clear text traffic is Enabled For App [android:usesCleartextTraffic=true]
reason: Flag is real (aapt2 confirms). But the only endpoint in the whole artefact is https://ninja.secops.group and the app pins it. A permission to send cleartext that is never exercised is a hardening note, not an exposure. Merged into the hardening table.
evidence: aapt2 dump xmltree: usesCleartextTraffic=true; strings over classes.dex: exactly one URL, https-only

reason: exported=true with no readPermission and no writePermission. openFile() opens new File(getFilesDir(), uri.getLastPathSegment()) - any app on the device can read any file directly under files/, including the secrets.db the Application writes at startup.
evidence: manifest: exported=true, no permissions; LeakyFileProvider.java:40 openFile(); CmpenApp.java:17 writes files/../databases/secrets.db

claim: Content Provider (org.android.cmpen.FlagProvider) is Protected by a permission [readPermission=org.android.cmpen.permission.ACCESS_FLAG]
reason: The scanner rated this INFO because a permission is present. The permission is declared IN THE SAME MANIFEST with protectionLevel=0x00000000 = normal, so any app may request and receive it at install time. The guard is decorative.

claim: Activity (org.android.cmpen.MainActivity) is not Protected. An intent-filter exists.
reason: It is the LAUNCHER activity. Every installed app has exactly one of these and it is exported because the platform must be able to start it. Reporting it is the most common single artefact in scanner-derived reports.
Real and exported. Not yet a finding: what an unprivileged caller gains has not been demonstrated. Deferred to dynamic - am start from the shell is NOT proof, because shell is not an app.
Merged into V017. Export is what makes the WebView bridge remotely reachable; on its own it is surface. One finding, two facts - not two findings.
Exported and excludeFromRecents. Worth ten minutes; not a finding until the Activity is shown to disclose something to its caller.
Merged into V010; the same component reported twice under two rules.

claim: Activity (org.android.cmpen.DeepLinkActivity) is a Browsable Activity - ctfapp://open/admin
reason: Browsable custom scheme reachable from any web page. The Activity compares two URI query parameters against string literals present in the DEX and grants access on match. The scanner rated it INFO because it fires on the FILTER; the finding is what the code does with the URI.
evidence: manifest: BROWSABLE + scheme=ctfapp host=open path=/admin; DeepLinkActivity.java:25-27 compares ref/token to literals

claim: Application Data can be Backed up [android:allowBackup=true]
reason: allowBackup=true with no dataExtractionRules and no fullBackupContent, so the whole private directory is in scope - including databases/secrets.db. Severity is Low and not Medium because the precondition is USB debugging plus an unlocked device.
evidence: aapt2: allowBackup=true; no dataExtractionRules attribute anywhere in the manifest

claim: App can be installed on a vulnerable Android version. [minSdk=24]
reason: The rule fires on an integer. It names no weakness, no CVE and no platform behaviour this application depends on. minSdk is a support decision. Reporting it wastes the client's remediation budget and costs you credibility on the items that matter.

Signer DN is C=US O=Android CN=Android Debug. The debug signing key ships with the Android SDK and is identical on every developer machine, so anyone can produce a package the platform will accept as an update to this one.
evidence: apksigner verify -v --print-certs: 'Signer #1 certificate DN: C=US, O=Android, CN=Android Debug'; SHA-256 5b571963...4d3266

reason: Direction error. A MISSING v1 signature on a minSdk 24 app is a compatibility note. The security-relevant case is the inverse - v1 present without v2, which is the Janus exposure. Reporting this as a weakness inverts the actual risk.
evidence: apksigner: v1 False, v2 True, v3 False

claim: Files may contain hardcoded sensitive information like usernames, passwords, keys etc.
reason: One rule, five files, five different answers. Split into V015a-e below rather than reported as one High. This is the single most misused MobSF finding.
A username, and a default one. Not a credential.

The value is a digest, not a password - so 'hardcoded password' is wrong. The finding is the DESIGN: an unsalted single-round SHA-256 password verifier evaluated on the client, which can be brute-forced offline and bypassed entirely by patching the comparison.
Decodes in one command to a plaintext token, and it is returned by an exported provider's query(). Encoding is not encryption. Severity comes from V003/V004 reachability, not from the literal.

Ciphertext, not plaintext (decodes to 48 high-entropy bytes). Ciphertext in an artefact is only a finding when the key is in the artefact too - and here it is: the key is derived from a user-supplied string via one SHA-256 round. Merged into V016.

claim: XOR-obfuscated base64 in MemorySecret and WebAppInterface
reason: g.b() base64-decodes then XORs every byte with 0x5A. That is obfuscation, defeated in two lines of Python. The getAuthToken() value is exposed to page JavaScript through the WebView bridge, which is where its severity comes from.

claim: The App uses ECB mode in Cryptographic encryption algorithm
reason: AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding confirmed at B/g.java:28. The scanner is right and INCOMPLETE: the worse defect is on the two lines above it - the key is the first 16 bytes of a single unsalted SHA-256 of a caller-supplied string, with no KDF and no IV. No MobSF rule covers that, so it appears in no report.

WebViewActivity is exported, reads its URL from an Intent extra (load_url) with no validation, enables JavaScript, and binds WebAppInterface as 'AndroidBridge'. Any app on the device can point the WebView at a page it controls and call getAuthToken() from JavaScript. All three preconditions are in one 22-line file.
evidence: WebViewActivity.java:14 setJavaScriptEnabled(true); :15 addJavascriptInterface; :17 getStringExtra("load_url"); :20 loadUrl; manifest exported=true

claim: This app has enabled JavaScript in WebView
reason: Merged into V017. setJavaScriptEnabled(true) alone is not a finding - most WebViews need it. It is a precondition of the bridge finding, not a second finding.
Real and meaningless on its own. Base64 appears in essentially every application. It matters here only as part of V015e, where it is already reported.

Rule mis-fires. CmpenApp.java:17 does not create a temporary file; it writes databases/secrets.db, a permanent file in the private data directory. The construct is real, the CATEGORY is wrong, and the interesting fact - that the file is reachable through V003 - is not what the rule says.

An SPKI pin: the base64 SHA-256 of a public key. It is published in every TLS handshake the server performs. Listing it as a hardcoded secret is a category error and it is one the tool makes on every pinning application.
evidence: classify_secret -> SPKI pin; b/h.java:24 CertificatePinner add

reason: Same value as V015b. The secrets section and the code section report the same literal twice; count it once.
Ciphertext. Merged into V015d/V016.

The appsec scorecard restates the manifest, code and certificate sections. Counting it as extra items is how a 12-item scan becomes a 39-item report. Validate the underlying section; never quote the scorecard.
evidence: see the corresponding manifest/code/certificate rows above

claim: This application does not implement certificate pinning
reason: The report is wrong in the dangerous direction. The app DOES pin: one SPKI value for ninja.secops.group, configured on a static OkHttpClient. The detector looked for the type name okhttp3.CertificatePinner; R8 renamed it to m.e/m.d/m.g and the name-based rule found nothing. Grepping for the 43-character pin value finds it immediately. Compare with v1.0 of the same app, which is unobfuscated and where the same detector succeeds.
evidence: grep -a -o -E 'sha256/[A-Za-z0-9+/]{43}=' classes.dex -> 1 value; b/h.java:20-27 static OkHttpClient with the pinner; 36-CertificatePinning/scripts/pinning-surface.py reports 'PIN CONFIGURED at 1 layer(s)'

claim: SHA-256 used directly as a key derivation function
reason: Nothing in the report mentions it. There is no MobSF rule for 'hash used as a KDF', so the defect with the widest blast radius in this application appears nowhere in the scan. Found by reading the file the ECB rule pointed at.

No rule fired. getLastPathSegment() limits classic ../ traversal because a segment cannot contain an unencoded slash - but the provider still opens any file directly under files/ for any caller, and %2F handling must be tested on a device before either sentence is written.
Neither the report nor any artefact-based tool can enumerate receivers registered with registerReceiver(). Recorded in the report's limits section rather than assumed to be empty.
evidence: 29-BroadcastReceivers measured 299 of 431 actions (69%) with no manifest-declared receiver on a live device
